Analytical stance under test: Stance 180 - Quantization changes the weight-bytes term but not the collective-bytes term, so it moves the two axes by different amounts.

Common frame (applies to every stance below).
Assumptions (must be restated by the answering engineer, not inherited silently):
A1. Single node, 8 GPUs, NVLink/NVSwitch intra-node; inter-node paths only appear where a stance says so explicitly.
A2. Decode-dominant, latency-sensitive serving: the SLO is TTFT p95 and TPOT (inter-token latency) p95, never a mean.
A3. Model weights fit in aggregate HBM with at least 20% KV-cache headroom at target concurrency.
A4. Exactly one variable moves per arm: no simultaneous change of quantization, batching policy, or speculative decoding.
Mechanism, stated plainly:
- Tensor parallelism (TP) shards every layer's GEMMs. Each transformer block needs two all-reduces (after attention out-projection and after the MLP down-projection), so decode carries L * 2 * allreduce_latency of synchronous cost, where L is the layer count. TP is latency-additive in collectives but capacity- and bandwidth-multiplying: per-GPU weight bytes and per-GPU KV bytes both fall by the TP degree.
- Pipeline parallelism (PP) shards layers into stages. Per token it adds only (PP-1) small point-to-point hidden-state sends, which are cheap, but a single request serializes through all stages and the bubble fraction is (PP-1)/(micro_batches + PP-1). At low concurrency there are too few in-flight micro-batches to fill the pipeline, so PP loses badly on single-request latency.
Boundary conditions that flip the answer:
- B1. On NVLink-class fabric, small-message all-reduce latency is in the single-digit microseconds and TP up to 8 is normally latency-viable. Over PCIe-only or across nodes on RoCE/IB the same collective's latency floor rises roughly an order of magnitude and TP stops paying past TP=2 (ESTIMATE; derivation: decode all-reduce payload is hidden_size * dtype_bytes per token per layer, which is small, so the collective is latency-bound rather than bandwidth-bound and the per-hop latency floor dominates).
- B2. If the model cannot fit on one GPU, sharding is mandatory and the question reduces to which axis, not whether.
- B3. Under high, steady concurrency the PP bubble amortizes and PP becomes competitive on throughput per GPU while still losing on single-request latency.
Default recommendation: use TP inside the node up to the point where collective cost stops being repaid by reduced per-GPU memory traffic; use PP only to cross a node boundary or to fit a model TP alone cannot fit. PP is not a latency optimization.

Only values read out of named benchmark artifacts may be labelled MEASURED. This review reports no MEASURED values, because no benchmark was executed for it.

Low-precision weights shrink the per-GPU parameter footprint and the weight-load time of every matmul, but a tensor-parallel all-reduce still carries activations whose element count is fixed by hidden size and batch, and which are frequently kept at higher precision for numerical safety. The compute side therefore shrinks while the communication side does not, which raises the collective's share of the decode step and erodes the tensor layout's margin. Falsifiable hypothesis H180: converting weights from sixteen-bit to eight-bit at fixed layout reduces the tensor arm's step time by less than the reduction in weight bytes would predict, and the residual gap is accounted for by the unchanged collective time measured on the device timeline (ESTIMATE; derivation: step time is the sum of a weight-bandwidth-bound term that scales with weight bytes and a collective term that does not, so shrinking only the first term produces a sub-proportional total speedup). Controlled experiment: run both layouts at each precision with identical kernels and batch shapes, attribute step time into collective and compute on the device timeline, and report an accuracy parity check at each precision so a speedup bought with quality loss is visible. Rollback gate: a precision change is not promoted unless the parity check stays inside the declared tolerance and the layout ordering is re-confirmed at the new precision, since the ordering may have flipped.

When prefill and decode run on separate pools, each pool can pick its own parallel layout: prefill is compute-dense and batch-rich, so it tolerates pipeline stages and even cross-node hops; decode is latency-bound and collective-sensitive, so it wants the tightest intra-node tensor group. Forcing one layout across both phases optimises a weighted average that neither phase actually experiences. The cost shifts to the KV handoff between pools, which becomes a new critical-path transfer. Falsifiable hypothesis H181: a disaggregated deployment with per-phase layouts beats the best single-layout co-located deployment on both TTFT and TPOT at the same GPU count, unless the measured KV transfer time per request exceeds the prefill-decode interference it removes (ESTIMATE; derivation: disaggregation removes prefill-decode contention within a step but adds one KV transfer per request, so the net sign is decided by comparing those two measured quantities directly). Controlled experiment: measure per-request KV transfer bytes and latency on the handoff path, measure prefill-induced TPOT inflation in the co-located arm, and compare the two arms at equal total GPU count rather than equal per-pool count. Rollback gate: if measured KV transfer latency exceeds the declared fraction of the TTFT budget, disaggregation is reverted to co-located serving rather than absorbed as an unowned regression.

Once KV blocks are pooled, transferred between nodes or tiered into host memory or SSD, the decode path acquires a dependency on a storage and network system with its own queueing, hit rate and tail behaviour. A layout benchmark that keeps all KV resident in device memory measures a system without that dependency and therefore cannot bound production tail latency. The relevant question becomes whether a block arrives before the step that needs it. Falsifiable hypothesis H182: with a pooled or tiered KV layer enabled, p99 TPOT is governed by block-fetch stall time rather than by the parallel layout, so the two layouts converge at p99 while remaining separated at p50 (ESTIMATE; derivation: a stall waits on a transfer whose latency is set by the storage tier and fabric, a term that is added identically to both layouts and that dominates the tail once its magnitude exceeds the layout difference). Controlled experiment: instrument block-fetch hit rate, fetch latency distribution and per-step stall time, run both layouts with the tiered layer enabled and disabled, and report p50 and p99 separately for each of the four cells. Rollback gate: if measured stall time exceeds the declared share of the TPOT budget, the tiering tier is disabled or capacity is added before any layout conclusion is drawn from that configuration.

In a control-plane-managed deployment, request placement, replica selection, KV-aware routing and scale-up latency all sit on the observed end-to-end path. A layout that looks worse may simply be receiving worse routing, and a layout that looks better may be benefiting from a warmer replica set. Benchmarking through the control plane without pinning its policy conflates engine behaviour with orchestration behaviour. Falsifiable hypothesis H183: pinning routing to a fixed replica and disabling autoscaling changes the measured gap between layouts by more than the run-to-run dispersion, which would prove the control plane was contributing a material share of the observed difference (ESTIMATE; derivation: router choices redistribute queueing delay across replicas, and queueing delay at high utilisation is a large and highly variable component of end-to-end latency relative to per-step engine differences). Controlled experiment: run the layout comparison twice, once directly against a pinned engine replica and once through the control plane with its policy recorded, and report the delta between the two as the control-plane contribution. Rollback gate: no layout claim is published from control-plane-mediated numbers unless the pinned-replica run reproduces the same ordering; otherwise the finding is reclassified as a routing finding.

A tensor-parallel group is a synchronous unit; one dead rank stalls the collective and takes the whole replica down until the group is rebuilt. A pipeline arrangement is also synchronous within a replica, but its stage boundaries give a coarser, more restartable unit and a smaller blast radius when replicas are packed per node. Availability, not just latency, is therefore a function of the layout. Falsifiable hypothesis H184: injecting a single-rank fault produces a longer measured time-to-recovered-serving in the tensor arm than an equivalent single-stage fault in the pipeline arm, at equal replica count, because group reconstruction spans more coupled processes (ESTIMATE; derivation: recovery time scales with the number of processes that must be restarted and re-synchronised before the first token can be served, which is larger for a tightly coupled collective group). Controlled experiment: run identical fault-injection drills against both arms, killing one process per drill, and measure time from fault to first successfully served token plus the number of requests failed, repeated enough times to report a distribution. Rollback gate: a layout whose measured recovery time exceeds the availability budget is not promoted regardless of its latency advantage, and the drill is re-run after any topology change.
